chapter.title: JPEG File Format
chapter.par: JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) format is good choice for storing images with large number of colors and without sharp edges. It uses lossy compression which can greatly reduce size of image file. Imaging uses Independent JPEG Group's jpeglib library (version 6b) to load and save JPEG files. It was translated to Pascal by Jacques Nomssi Nzali. Optionally, libjpeg-turbo shared library can be used instead for much faster loading and saving (see JPEG Codecs below).

row.td: ifA8R8G8B8 (converted to RGB, without color management)

chapter.par: What to expect from various kinds of JPEG files:

blist.li: Baseline and progressive files with any chroma subsampling are loaded. Files are saved with 4:2:0, 4:2:2, or 4:4:4 subsampling, baseline or progressive.
Files without JFIF header (only with EXIF and/or Adobe marker, as written by some cameras and Adobe products, or with no application markers at all) are loaded like any other JPEG.

Resolution (DPI) is read from and written to JFIF header only. EXIF data is not interpreted, so files that have their resolution only in EXIF are loaded without it. EXIF and other metadata are not preserved when the image is saved again.

Damaged files: when an error is found in the image data the part decoded so far is returned where possible (always with libjpeg-turbo; with Pascal codec in Free Pascal and 32 bit Delphi, exception is raised in other Delphi targets). Files with damaged headers raise exception.

Arithmetic coded files can not be loaded by the Pascal codec (jpeglib 6b does not have the decoder). They are rare, most software including web browsers can not show them either. libjpeg-turbo loads them (unless the library was built without arithmetic coding support).
Lossless JPEG and files with 12 bit samples are not supported.
Alpha channel is not part of JPEG format. Images with alpha are converted to 24 bit RGB when saved. Use JNG format (JPEG compressed colors with separate alpha channel) if you need both.

chapter.par: Pascal translation of jpeglib is always compiled in (the one bundled with Imaging, or the one shipped with Free Pascal in Lazarus LCL applications). If you define JPEG_USE_TURBO_DYNLIB symbol (in project options or in ImagingOptions.inc) Imaging also looks for libjpeg-turbo shared library with TurboJPEG API when the first JPEG image is loaded or saved: turbojpeg.dll in Windows, libturbojpeg.so.0 in Linux, and libturbojpeg.0.dylib in macOS. Version 2.0 or newer is needed, older libraries are ignored. When the library is found it is used for all JPEG loading and saving (also for JPEG data inside JNG and MNG files), otherwise the Pascal codec is used, so the application works without the library too.

Both codecs give the same results: decoded pixels and saved files are identical. libjpeg-turbo is several times faster though (about 3x when loading and 10x when saving large images) and it is more tolerant to damaged files. It needs the whole file in memory when loading. Functions JpegBackend and TryLoadTurboJpegLibrary (to load the library from specific location) in ImagingJpegLib unit tell and control which codec is used.

When working with JPEG files you can find useful some options which can be set by SetOption function and their current values can be get by GetOption function. Or you can set them by modifying properties of TJpegFileFormat class.

row.td: JPEG compression quality used when saving images. Higher value means worse compression/better image quality/larger file size. Default value is 90.

Indicates whether JPEG is saved as progressive or not. Progressive JPEG rearranges the stored data into a series of scans of increasing quality. In situations where a JPEG file is transmitted across a slow communications link, a decoder can generate a low-quality image very quickly from the first scan, then gradually improve the displayed quality as more scans are received. Default value is 0 (False).

Chroma subsampling used when saving color JPEG images. Color (chroma) components are stored with half horizontal and vertical resolution (4:2:0), half horizontal resolution (4:2:2), or full resolution (4:4:4) compared to luminance. Less subsampling preserves sharp color edges better but gives larger files. Ignored for grayscale images. Default value is 0 (4:2:0).
